Whole-Lesson Orientation

This tab is a map of the lecture. The lesson proper begins in the next tab.

What this lecture builds toward

  • General virus properties: acellular, submicroscopic, obligate intracellular particles with DNA or RNA genomes.
  • Structure: genome, capsid, optional envelope, spikes, and viral proteins determine entry, classification, and laboratory behavior.
  • Genome strategy: polarity and the Baltimore Classification organize how a virus reaches mRNA and viral protein synthesis.
  • Replication: Attachment → Penetration → Uncoating → Synthesis → Assembly → Release.
  • Host-cell outcome: infection may be abortive, lytic, or persistent.
  • Laboratory detection: culture, hemadsorption, hemagglutination, nucleic acid detection, cytopathic effects, and embryonated chick embryo growth are covered.

Lecture anchorWhat to remember
VirionComplete infectious unit. Naked virions have genome + capsid. Enveloped virions add an envelope.
SpikesGlycoproteins that bind host receptors and help determine tissue or viral tropism.
Polarity(+) RNA can function as mRNA. (-) RNA needs RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to produce (+) viral mRNA.

Must Know
All viruses must direct the synthesis of mRNA to produce proteins.
All viral protein synthesis depends completely on the host cell translational machinery.

General Characteristics of Viruses

p. 1

Viruses are described first by what they lack, their size, and their dependence on living cells.

Core characteristics

  • Acellular: they do not possess cell organelles and metabolic processes required by prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
  • Not considered living things in the lecture framework.
  • Submicroscopic: not visible by compound light microscopy and not demonstrated by Gram staining or other light microscopy techniques.
  • Electron microscopy is required for visualization.
  • They have no genes that encode protein synthesis, energy production, or membrane biosynthesis.
  • Obligate intracellular parasites: outside living cells they cannot self-replicate.
  • Resistant to antibiotics.
  • Replication can be inhibited by antiviral agents and interferon.
Size of cells versus virions
Cell or particleSizeLecture note
Prokaryotic cells1–10 μmExample: bacteria
Eukaryotic cells10–100 μmExamples: fungi and human cells
Virions20–300 nmSmall enough to pass through bacterial filters. Filtration alone is not enough for removal in water.

Interferon as an Antiviral Defense

p. 1

The lecture presents interferon as a natural defense signal between infected and neighboring host cells.

Lecture sequence

  1. A virus infects a host cell.
  2. The IFN gene is activated.
  3. Interferon is released outside the infected cell.
  4. Neighboring cells receive the signal and produce antiviral proteins.
  5. These antiviral proteins interfere with viral multiplication and help destroy viral particles.

Virus Taxonomy

p. 2

The lecture uses the universal scheme developed by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses.

ICTV framework

  • The naming system is based on names established in 1966 by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses.
  • The ICTV developed a single universal scheme for viruses infecting animals, plants, fungi, bacteria, and archaea.
  • The lecture lists the usable taxa as Order, Suborder, Family, Subfamily, Genus, Subgenus, and Species.

Virion

p. 3

A virion is the entire infectious unit and may be organized as a naked nucleocapsid or an enveloped particle.

Virion organization
Virion typePartsKey description
Naked nucleocapsid virion2 partsCapsid + nucleic acid genome
Enveloped virion3 partsCapsid + nucleic acid genome + envelope with protruding spikes

Envelope

p. 3

The viral envelope is a host-derived phospholipid bilayer acquired during budding and release.

Envelope properties

  • Phospholipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane.
  • Produced during budding and release.
  • All enveloped viruses derive their envelope from host cell membrane, with the lecture exception that Herpes obtains it from the nuclear membrane.
  • The envelope contains inserted viral proteins called peplomeres.
  • Peplomeres are important for attachment and for induction of protective immunity.
Naked DNA and naked RNA viruses
Naked DNANaked RNA
ParvoviridaePicornaviridae
PapillomaviridaeReoviridae
PolyomaviridaeCaliciviridae
AdenoviridaeHepeviridae

AttributeEnveloped virusesNaked viruses
Injurious agentsSensitive to ether, alcohol, detergent, and dry heatResistant to ether and other environmental factors
Mode of transmissionDirect contact
Example: HIV		Fecal–oral route
Example: poliovirus

Spikes and Receptor Binding

p. 3

Spikes are glycoprotein structures protruding from the viral surface or envelope that bind specific host-cell receptors and facilitate entry.

Examples from the lecture

  • Influenza hemagglutinin binds the host-cell glycan chain.
  • SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 spike protein attaches to ACE2 and the TMPRSS2 co-receptor.
  • HIV gp120 attaches to CD4+.
  • CCR5 or CXCR4 act as HIV co-receptors and help with attachment.
  • In patients with HIV, the lecture notes a decrease in CD4+.

Capsid and Nucleocapsid

p. 4

The capsid is the protein coat around the genome. The nucleocapsid is the genome plus the capsid.

Kinds of capsid symmetry
SymmetryLecture descriptionExamples or pattern
IcosahedralPolyhedral or cubic with 20 flat sidesMostly DNA and (+) sense RNA
May be naked or inside an envelope
HelicalSpiral or cylindrical, forming a helixEnveloped (-) sense RNA
May be shown as a coiled nucleocapsid or inside an envelope
ComplexLacks the usual capsid symmetry featuresPoxvirus with dumbbell-shaped core and bilateral bodies
Rabies virus described as bullet-shaped

Viral Proteins and Their Functions

p. 4

The lecture links viral proteins to attachment, replication, structure, serotyping, genome protection, and the envelope–nucleocapsid interface.

Six viral proteins and functions
Viral proteinFunction
Structural proteinsAttachment to host-cell receptor
EnzymesExamples include DNA or RNA polymerase
Matrix proteinInteraction between nucleocapsid and envelope
Antigenic proteinSerotyping of different strains
CapsidProvides structural symmetry, including helical or icosahedral patterns
Protein in the envelopeProtects the viral genome against inactivation by nucleases
Key Differentiator
The simplest viruses contain only enough RNA or DNA to encode about four proteins.
The most complex can encode about 100–200 proteins.

Glycoproteins, Tropism, and Viral Enzymes

p. 4

Glycoprotein spikes must interact with a host receptor for entry, making them central to tissue or viral tropism.

Lecture examples

  • KSHV or Herpesvirus 8: viral glycoproteins gB and gHgL interact with the human host receptor CD98.
  • Influenza HA can agglutinate red blood cells and is used in detecting influenza virus in patient serum in the lecture discussion.
  • RNA polymerase: described as copying a DNA sequence into an RNA sequence during transcription. The lecture also notes that influenza requires an RNA-dependent polymerase.
  • Reverse transcriptase: in retroviruses, makes a DNA copy of viral RNA during replication and transformation of the host cell.

Matrix Protein, Antigenic Variants, and Capsomeres

p. 5

Matrix protein

  • Found between the envelope and nucleocapsid.
  • May have enzymatic activities and biologic functions related to infection.

HBV antigenic variants

  • HBsAg: hepatitis B surface antigen.
  • HBcAg: hepatitis B core antigen.
  • HBeAg is also listed.
  • The lecture states that these antigens help identify antibodies produced by the patient and help determine antigenic characteristics.
  • The lecture associates HBsAg with the acute stage and HBcAg with the chronic stage.

Capsomeres

  • Capsomeres are a finite number of protein subunits surrounding the capsid.
  • Viral proteins also provide structural symmetry and protect the genome from nucleases.

The lecture describes transcription as information copied into RNA and translation as protein synthesis using host cellular machinery.

Baltimore Classification

p. 7

David Baltimore introduced the classification in 1971. It groups viruses by genome type and method of replication.

Core rule

  • Seven groups are used in the Baltimore Classification.
  • All viruses must direct the synthesis of mRNA to make proteins.
  • All viral protein synthesis depends completely on the translational machinery of the host cell.
Seven Baltimore groups
CategoryGroupGenome
DNA virusesIdsDNA, DNA (+/-)
DNA virusesIIssDNA, DNA (+)
RNA virusesIIIdsRNA, RNA (+/-)
RNA virusesIVssRNA (+), RNA (+)
RNA virusesVssRNA (-), RNA (-)
RetrovirusesVIssRNA, RNA (+)
RetrovirusesVIIdsDNA, DNA (+/-)

Group I: dsDNA

p. 7

Group I follows the conventional dsDNA → mRNA → viral protein pathway.

Replication logic

  1. The genome has the same polarity as the host cell it infects.
  2. DNA-dependent RNA polymerase produces mRNA from viral DNA.
  3. The mRNA is translated to produce viral protein.
  4. DNA-dependent DNA polymerase from the virus or host copies the (+) and (-) strands to produce dsDNA viral genome.
❗ Must Know Mnemonic
Group I viruses are HAPPPy.
Herpesviridae. Adenoviridae. Papillomaviridae. Poxviridae. Polyomaviridae.

Group II: ssDNA (+)

p. 7

The lecture states that Group II contains one family, Parvoviridae.

Parvovirus pathway

  • Parvoviridae is the only family listed for this group.
  • Parvovirus B19 is given as a cause of fifth disease.
  • The ssDNA genome first forms a double-stranded replicative form.
  • DNA-dependent RNA polymerase uses the negative strand to produce positive viral mRNA.
  • DNA-dependent DNA polymerase from the virus or host copies the negative DNA strand to produce the single-stranded positive DNA viral genome.

Group III: dsRNA (+/-)

p. 8

A viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase acts as both replicase and transcriptase.

Reoviridae pattern

  • RNA-dependent RNA polymerase acts as a replicase for genome replication and a transcriptase for mRNA transcription.
  • The (+) strand inside dsRNA cannot be used directly as mRNA because it is hydrogen-bonded to the negative strand.
  • The lecture lists only Reoviridae, with rotavirus as the example.
  • Rotavirus is described as causing diarrhea in children, being non-enveloped, not spiked, having a triple-layered capsid, and possessing a segmented RNA genome.

Group IV: ssRNA (+)

p. 8

Positive single-stranded RNA can be translated as soon as the genome enters the cell.

Three-step logic in the lecture

  1. The (+) RNA genome functions directly as mRNA and is translated by the host ribosome.
  2. The translated products include RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which makes ss(-)RNA from the plus-stranded genome.
  3. The minus-stranded RNA serves as a template for new ss(+)RNA that can function as mRNA or become genomes in newly forming virus particles.
Group IV families
Group IV familiesExamples in lecture
CaliciviridaeNorwalk virus
CoronaviridaeSARS, MERS
HepeviridaeHepatitis E
PicornaviridaePolio, etc.
TogaviridaeRubella, etc.
FlaviviridaeDengue, etc.

Group V: ssRNA (-)

p. 8

Negative-strand RNA cannot be used as mRNA, so the virion must supply RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

Replication logic

  • The negative RNA genome is used as a template.
  • The virus must carry RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the capsid to make viral mRNA.
  • The negative template can be copied into a positive RNA template strand.
  • The positive RNA then serves as a template for production of new ss(-)RNA viral genomes.
Group V examples
Negative-strand family or virusExample
ArenavirusesLassa fever virus
BunyavirusesHanta fever virus
ParamyxovirusesMumps and measles
OrthomyxovirusesInfluenza
FilovirusesEbola and Marburg
RhabdovirusesRabies
Delta virusListed under Group V, not a family
❗ Must Know
Always Bring Polymerase Or Fail Replication is repeated as the mnemonic for Group V negative-strand RNA viruses.

Group VI: ssRNA (+) Retrovirus

p. 9

The genome is positive-strand RNA, but unlike ordinary Group IV positive RNA it is not used directly as mRNA.

Why “retrovirus”

  1. Reverse transcriptase copies the positive RNA genome into ssDNA.
  2. Reverse transcriptase then helps produce dsDNA.
  3. The DNA is incorporated into the host-cell genome using integrase.
  4. Subsequent transcription and translation produce viral proteins.

Examples: HIV and HTLV.

Group VII: dsDNA (+/-) Retrovirus

p. 9

The lecture calls Group VII a “gapped virus” because the dsDNA genome is single-stranded in one part.

Hepadnaviridae pathway

  • Family: Hepadnaviridae.
  • Example: Hepatitis B virus.
  • The gapped dsDNA is filled in and forms a closed circle for production of viral mRNA.
  • Despite its DNA genome, the virus replicates through an ssRNA intermediate.
  • Reverse transcriptase converts the RNA intermediate back to DNA to reproduce the genome.
❗ Must Know
Group VII = gapped dsDNA virus in the lecture.
It uses an RNA intermediate and reverse transcriptase despite having a DNA genome.

Retroviruses Compared

p. 9
Summary of retroviruses
FeatureType VIType VII
GenomessRNA (+)dsDNA (+/-)
FamilyRetroviridaeHepadnaviridae
VirusesHIV, HTLVHepatitis B
StructureEnveloped, icosahedralEnveloped, icosahedral

Viral Replication Cycle

p. 10

The lecture compresses the replication cycle into the six-step mnemonic APUSAR.

Must Know Mnemonic
APUSAR = Attachment, Penetration, Uncoating, Synthesis, Assembly, Release.

1. Attachment or Adsorption

p. 10

Viral proteins on the capsid or envelope interact with specific host-cell receptors.

Attachment determines tropism

  • Viral spikes or surface proteins bind receptors on the host-cell surface.
  • Specificity determines host range and tissue tropism.
  • The lecture uses SARS and HIV as receptor-dependent attachment examples.

2. Penetration

p. 10

Penetration is the process by which a virus enters the host cell.

Penetration methods
MethodWho uses it in the lectureMechanism
Direct fusionSome enveloped virusesThe virion adsorbs and fuses with the host-cell membrane, releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm.
Viropexis
Receptor-mediated endocytosis		Several enveloped viruses and all naked virusesThe host membrane invaginates and encloses the virus in an endocytotic vesicle or endosome.

3. Uncoating

p. 11

Uncoating removes the capsid and exposes the viral nucleic acid.

Uncoating and the eclipse phase

  • Capsid degradation or removal is performed by viral or host enzymes.
  • The genome is released into the host cell.
  • This marks the start of the eclipse phase in the viral growth curve.
  • During the eclipse phase, infectious particles cannot be recovered from the collected specimen.

4. Synthesis

p. 11

This is where the viral genome is replicated and viral proteins are synthesized through transcription or translation.

Synthesis rules

  • Synthesis forms the basis of the Baltimore Classification.
  • The lecture states that DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus, except poxviruses.
  • The synthesis section states that RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm, except Orthomyxoviruses and retroviruses listed as HIV, HTLV, and Hep B.
  • Early proteins are nonstructural elements such as enzymes.
  • Late proteins are structural components such as envelope and glycoprotein.
Lecture-Specific Note
Later in the lecture summary, the RNA-virus table lists Orthomyxoviridae and Reoviridae as replication-location exceptions.
This reviewer preserves both lecture statements without reconciling them.

5. Assembly and 6. Release

p. 11

Assembly

  • Structural proteins, viral genomes, and viral enzymes are assembled into virus particles.
  • The viral genome is enclosed in the protein coat or capsid.

Release

  • Budding: produces enveloped viruses from the host-cell membrane.
  • Lysis: used by most naked viruses.
  • Lysis may lead to apoptosis, host-cell death, and viral release.

Viral Growth Curve

p. 11

The lecture labels phases from entry through a final cytopathic-effect phase.

Viral growth curve phases
PhaseLecture labelWhat happens
0EntryVirus enters the host cell.
1DeclineVirus decreases in number but continues to function.
2Eclipse periodNo virus is detectable inside the cell. Viral component synthesis occurs as proteins and genome are being made.
3Exponential or rise periodProgeny virus increases exponentially for 8–72 hours.
4Latent period or plateauNo additional increase in virus yield occurs. The lecture gives a yield of 100–10,000 virions per cell. Virus may be intracellular or extracellular.
5Cytoplasmic effectMarked derangement of cell function leading to lysis and cell death, including cell-size and shape changes.

Abortive Infection

p. 11

An abortive infection occurs when the host cell is non-permissive or the infecting virus is defective.

Hepatitis D example

  • No replication and no virions produced in a non-permissive situation.
  • Hepatitis D is the lecture example of a defective infecting virus.
  • Without hepatitis B, hepatitis D cannot replicate.
  • The lecture calls it a virozoid or satellite.
  • With hepatitis B present, it can replicate.

Lytic Infection

p. 12

Lytic infection is characterized by viral progeny production together with host-cell damage.

Lytic pattern

  • Viruses replicate and produce progeny.
  • There is cell death and cytopathic effect.
  • Cellular protein and nucleic-acid synthesis are inhibited.
  • Evidence can include thickening or swelling, inclusion bodies, and syncytial bodies.

Persistent Infection

p. 12

In persistent infection, infected cells survive viral replication and only a small number of viral particles may be produced with little or no cytopathic effect.

Three persistent-infection patterns
TypeLecture descriptionExample
Viral transformationViral infection or gene product induces unregulated cellular growth and tumor formation by oncogenic viruses.No single example specified in this section
Chronic infectionLow-level viral production without immune clearance.Hepatitis B or hepatitis C
Latent infectionViral genetic material remains in host cells and can be activated later.VZ virus or HSV3 dormant in nerve ganglia, with later reactivation

Hemadsorption Link to Cell Culture

p. 12

Some viruses give infected cells receptors that can bind mammalian red blood cells.

Hemadsorption

  • Hemadsorption means infected cells acquire the ability to stick to mammalian red blood cells.
  • The lecture figure shows this together with syncytial formation caused by mumps virus.

Adsorption of RBCs and Hemagglutination

p. 13

The lecture uses red-cell reactions as visual evidence of certain viral properties.

Hemagglutination interpretation

  • When virus is present, hemagglutinin attaches to RBCs and produces hemagglutination.
  • A negative reaction shows a compact dot or “button” at the bottom of the well or tube.
  • In the lecture serial-dilution example, samples 1, 2, and 3 remain positive at 1:128.
  • Sample 4 is described as negative from the start, showing the button pattern.

Cytopathic Effects

p. 13

Cytopathic effects are visible host-cell changes produced by viral infection.

Major cytopathic events in the lecture
CPEWhat it looks likeExamples
Syncytial formationInfected cells fuse with neighboring cells, creating a multinucleated enlarged cell. Normal cells remain separate.RSV
Measles virus

Viral Growth in Embryonated Chick Embryo

p. 14

The lecture describes growth in a live chick embryo and detection by pocks, hemagglutination, or inclusion bodies.

What can be detected

  • Pocks on CAM, meaning growth on the chorio-allantoic membrane.
  • Hemagglutination, used for influenza.
  • Inclusion bodies.

Amniotic and Allantoic Inoculation

p. 14

Procedure described in the lecture

  • Inject 0.2 mL of virus into the amniotic fluid.
  • Pull the syringe to the area of allantoic fluid and inject 0.2 mL.
  • For influenza, extract allantoic material and test it for hemagglutination.
  • Positive viral growth produces hemagglutination in the lecture description.

Chorio-Allantoic Membrane Inoculation

p. 14

CAM inoculation is used in the lecture for suspected herpes simplex virus or pox virus.

CAM readout

  • A hole is made in the chorio-allantoic membrane and the specimen is applied.
  • After a few days, a positive test shows pock formation that appears as white dots.

❗ Red-Exclamation Content
BOAR = Bunyavirus, Orthomyxovirus, Arenavirus, Reovirus. These are the segmented RNA-virus groups emphasized in the lecture.
Always Bring Polymerase Or Fail Replication = Arenavirus, Bunyavirus, Paramyxovirus, Orthomyxovirus, Filovirus, Rhabdovirus. These negative-strand RNA viruses must bring RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Baltimore Classification has 7 groups.
Group I = HAPPPy: Herpesviridae, Adenoviridae, Papillomaviridae, Poxviridae, Polyomaviridae.
Group VII is the gapped dsDNA group and uses an RNA intermediate plus reverse transcriptase.
Rapid Recall
Virion = complete infectious unit.
Nucleocapsid = genome + capsid.
Enveloped virion = capsid + genome + envelope with spikes.
Spikes are glycoproteins that bind host receptors and help determine tissue tropism.
Naked viruses are more resistant to environmental factors and can withstand gastric acidity.
Enveloped viruses are sensitive to ether, alcohol, detergents, and dry heat.

Genome and Polarity

Genome and polarity anchors
AnchorFast recall
DNAMost are linear dsDNA. Parvoviridae = ssDNA. Papillomaviridae, Polyomaviridae, Hepadnaviridae = circular DNA. No negative-strand DNA.
RNAMost are linear ssRNA. Reoviridae = dsRNA. Delta virus = circular RNA. Orthomyxoviridae, Bunyaviridae, Arenaviridae = segmented ssRNA.
(+) RNASame polarity as mRNA. Can be used directly by host ribosomes.
(-) RNAAntisense to mRNA. Must carry RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to make (+) viral mRNA.
AmbisenseBoth (+) and (-) regions in one RNA segment. Arenaviridae and Bunyaviridae examples.

Baltimore in One Pass

Seven Baltimore groups
GroupGenomeOne-line strategy
IdsDNADNA → mRNA → protein
IIssDNA (+)Make a dsDNA replicative form first
IIIdsRNAVirion RNA-dependent RNA polymerase transcribes mRNA and replicates RNA
IVssRNA (+)Genome acts as mRNA, then makes a (-) template
VssRNA (-)Must bring polymerase to make (+) mRNA
VIssRNA (+) retrovirusReverse transcriptase makes DNA, then integrase inserts it into host genome
VIIGapped dsDNAUses an RNA intermediate and reverse transcriptase

APUSAR and Growth Curve

APUSAR
Attachment = receptor binding and tissue tropism.
Penetration = direct fusion or viropexis.
Uncoating = capsid removal and start of the eclipse phase.
Synthesis = genome replication and protein synthesis.
Assembly = structural proteins, genome, and enzymes form virions.
Release = enveloped viruses bud. Most naked viruses lyse the cell.
Viral growth curve
Growth phaseFast recall
0 EntryVirus enters.
1 DeclineVirus count decreases but virus continues to function.
2 EclipseNo detectable virus. Viral components are synthesized.
3 RiseExponential progeny increase for 8–72 h.
4 Plateau or latent periodNo additional yield increase. Lecture range 100–10,000 virions per cell.
5 Cytoplasmic effectCell derangement, shape change, lysis, and death.

Culture and Detection

Laboratory recall
TopicFast recall
Primary cultureVaccine production. Very expensive.
Semicontinuous cultureTransferred from primary cells. Also used for vaccine production.
Continuous cultureSerologic antigens and neutralizing antibody assays. Derived from cancer or immortalized cells.
PCRDenaturation → annealing → extension. Detects virus-specific nucleic acid.
Embryonated chick embryoLook for pocks on CAM, hemagglutination, or inclusion bodies.
Influenza allantoic growthExtract allantoic material and test for hemagglutination.
